SOLACE — A GRAPHIC NOVEL

Chaotic Designs

The light stays on.

Heavy. Quiet. Wet. Human. No camp, no victory without a cost.

The West Seattle Bridge is destroyed and the peninsula is sealed. Downtown glows across black water — close enough to see, unreachable enough to hurt. One man comes ashore in the dark with a knife, a damaged pistol, and the last coordinates of the woman he has to save. There is no road to her. He has to make one.

CHAPTER ONE — PROLOGUE: BEFORE THE WATER

Panel 1

A cheap motel room, years ago, desert light cutting through blinds. On the bed: a phone, face up, still lit. A man's hand — tattooed, steady — sets it down like it weighs more than a gun.

The order came down the way they all did. No name. No reason. Just a target.
This time the target was a teenage girl.

Panel 2

Flash inside the flash: a kitchen from an earlier job. An open fridge. A child's crayon drawing held up by a magnet — a house, a sun, stick figures holding hands. Ian's fist closes around a folded copy of it.

An earlier contract had already cracked him. He kept the drawing. He never said why.

Panel 3

Ian walks out of the motel into white desert glare, empty-handed, and doesn't look back. The phone stays on the bed, ringing.

The first order he ever refused. No speech. No scene. He just walked out.

Panel 4

White noon. A desert meet — one car, dust, heat shimmer. Ian stands waiting for a payout that was never coming. Nothing in frame moves except the heat.

The cartel doesn't let people quit with knowledge.

Panel 5

Ian falls backward into the dust. No muzzle flash drawn, no sound lettering — an empty white panel border, silence made visible. Dust hangs in the air where he stood.

A shot he never hears. The round carved bone instead of ending him.

Panel 6

Close: a gloved hand pressing two fingers to Ian's throat. His eyes are open and see nothing. Dust on his face like ash.

VOICE (distant, off-panel): "Leave him."

Panel 7

A county hospital room, months later, rendered in flat gray. Ian on the edge of a bed, relearning his own hands — fingers opening, closing, shaking. A scar crosses his skull where the round went in and out.

Months. Walking again. Seeing straight. Trusting his hands.

Panel 8

The same room, empty of everyone but him. He speaks to no one.

IAN: "No more jobs. No more people."

Panel 9

Ian walks out of the hospital into hard daylight wearing a filthy white ribbed tank and jeans — everything else he owned, he burned. He looks like a man with nothing, and for the first time in years, nothing owns him.

It was the first thing he'd worn in years that wasn't a uniform for killing. That's why he still wears it.

Panel 10

GOLDEN HOUR — the only warm memory in the book, and it hurts to look at. High-school Ian and Sara in a stolen rowboat on the Alki shallows at dusk, the city behind them whole and lit. Her hair tie is loose; her hair is down.

SARA: "When we leave — and we are leaving — where do we go?"

IAN (young): "Anywhere. I'll take you."

Panel 11

The same shoreline, matched framing, seventeen years later: burned, sealed, dark. The memory panel's warmth drains out of the page.

He never did take her. Hold that. It matters at the bridge.

Panel 12

NIGHT ZERO. The West Seattle Bridge tears apart in fire and falling concrete over black water. On the peninsula side, a ferry gate: a deckhand in an orange vest holds it open against a surge of people, waving one man through — Ian.

The night the world ended, a stranger held a gate for thirty seconds. It saved Ian's life. He never learned the man's name.

Panel 13

Days later, from the Alki shore: West Seattle dark and cut off, downtown Seattle glowing across the water like another planet. Smoke columns. No boats. No road.

The peninsula was sealed. Everyone inside was written off. Everyone but one woman, holding a refuge together in High Point — and one man who'd made a vow to an empty room, and was about to break it.

CHAPTER TWO — ACT I: ONE MAN COMES ASHORE

Panel 14

Night, rain. Black Puget Sound closes over Ian's head as he swims around the Alki barrier — only his eyes and the top of his scarred skull above the waterline, ice-blue eyes fixed on the dark shore.

Night Zero broke the vow. He went back for people. For Missy first.

Panel 15

Ian hauls himself over the seawall in the rain, soaked, knife at his belt, a damaged pistol in one hand. Seawall glass and saltwater open shallow cuts across his knuckles and knees. He doesn't notice.

A knife. A damaged pistol. And Missy's last coordinates. This is the last time Ian looks like the man who came ashore.

Panel 16

The Alki boardwalk, deserted and drowned-looking. Infected shapes drift between shuttered cafés — they were ferry crew, joggers, baristas. One in a torn orange vest stands apart, shoulder ripped where someone once grabbed it.

The infected are the neighborhood. Ian walks the long way around the one in the orange vest. He doesn't explain why. There is no one to explain to.

Panel 17

A dark café interior. A hand-cranked radio spits static. In the back room doorway, RAE MERCER — former ferry dispatcher, tired, unimpressed — watches Ian like a manifest she's checking twice.

RADIO (static, broken): "—peat… Missy's call sign… High Point… any station—"

RAE: "That's her sign. She's alive. High Point."

Panel 18

The café light comes on — weak, warm, gold — visible through wet glass from the dark street. Two silhouettes inside. Outside, rain.

RAE: "Good. Somebody sees that, they know the light stays on."

IAN: "Where?"

RAE: "No road. You'd have to make one."

Panel 19

Three-panel strip, three blocked ways out of Alki: a waterfront nest webbed across the Admiral climb; an evacuation wreck — a bus on its side — sealing the Junction ramp; a shoreline zone of sleeping Apex shapes, pale in the dark, that Ian must not wake.

Three emergencies. Pick one. The other two wait — and waiting changes who believes he's coming.

Panel 20

SALT LINE: fire on wet concrete — Ian burns the waterfront nest and holds the service stairs alone, shoulder braced, while the street burns gold and black behind him.

Panel 21

THE LONG RAMP: a winch cable screaming taut, an evacuation bus grinding aside inch by inch while Runners pour up the wreck toward Ian's light.

Panel 22

GHOST MILE: total darkness, a UV handlamp's violet edge. Ian moves through sleeping Apex shapes without touching the ground wrong, Eli's scouts bound and gagged ahead of him, breathing through their noses, praying quietly.

Panel 23

Back at the café, dawn the color of wet ash. Rae at the radio, a map weighted down by a coffee mug. Ian stands in the doorway, dripping, scarred knuckles wrapped in a strip of cloth.

RAE: "Road's open. One road. Rest is on you."

IAN: "What opens next?"

He spoke only in objectives. Rae refused to answer the question he was avoiding: what happens after he reaches Missy?

CHAPTER THREE — ACT II: THE CITY LEARNS HIS NAME

Panel 24

ADMIRAL DISTRICT, above the fog line. A damaged pressure substation, utility corridors full of trapped, stirring infected. Ian forces a door with his shoulder, holding a gate for a vent crew behind him.

Admiral taught him to hold weight for other people.

Panel 25

Close on Ian's left forearm as an arc flash crawls up it — he holds the breaker closed with his body while the crew vents the tunnel. The burn branches white against his tattoos.

The scar branches white. He stops rolling that sleeve down.

Panel 26

Two drained basements, a community hall lit gold, people eating at real tables. On a wall map, a new line is drawn: HIGH POINT PERIMETER. For three seconds, a woman's voice breaks through the radio static—

MISSY (radio, fragmented): "—keep walking—"

Then gone. He does.

Panel 27

THE JUNCTION, dusk over California Avenue — storefronts, awnings, a stalled bus, the street below filling with shadow. On the roofs: NIA BROOKS, courier, pointing with two fingers. A strip of white cloth tied to an antenna.

NIA: "White cloth, safe. Bent antenna, jump. No mark—"

IAN: "Listen."

NIA: "You learn fast."

Panel 28

A pharmacy skylight shatters inward. Below, bandits are coming through the front while Ian drops into the dark among the shelves, reaching for insulin as glass rains.

The medicine mattered more than the noise. It usually does.

Panel 29

Nia down on a rooftop, leg ruined, dusk going to night around her. Ian gets her across his shoulders without a word. Below the parapet, something pale begins to crawl.

NIA: "You can't carry me and fight."

IAN: "Watch."

Panel 30

The carry, full page energy in one frame: Ian crosses a stranded bus roof one-handed on a UV lamp, Nia on his back calling the route, an Apex sliding over the parapet behind them, claws sparking on wet metal. A Runner tears a ribbon of skin off Ian's shoulder as he throws Nia across the final gap.

NIA: "Gap — now!"

He cannot use his largest weapons. He uses himself instead. The bandage on that shoulder stays for two districts. Nia learns to check it without asking.

Panel 31

LINCOLN PARK — the green dark. Eli Cole, tracker, motionless in the rain under cedar, one hand raised. Between the trees: infected standing asleep in the wet, dozens, then hundreds toward the shore shelters.

ELI: "Gunfire here wakes all of it."

IAN: "How many?"

ELI: "You don't want the number."

Panel 32

THE STAND. Fire barrels and hooded lights at the shelter line, the horde arriving in waves through the trees — forty in the signature wave, sixty at the cap — and Ian in the gap with a rebar maul, silent, unhurried, a wall that bleeds. Blackberry thorns have opened his left cheek; one cut crosses his eyebrow.

Lincoln Park taught him killing is sometimes the loudest, worst solution. He killed anyway. Strangers flinch at him first now, and ask later.

Panel 33

MORGAN JUNCTION, Sora's clinic — gold light, cots, a queue of the hurt. DR. SORA KIM works without looking up. On the cots: the Alki lookout Ian spared. An Admiral family. A Junction civilian who was infected during a delay Ian chose.

SORA: "Stay for the names."

Every route converged at her clinic. Every decision he'd made was lying on a cot, looking at him.

Panel 34

Sora stitches a bandit-knife wound in Ian's thigh in a clinic corridor, flat and furious, while he stands there taking up the whole doorway.

SORA: "You keep paying in the same currency."

He doesn't argue. She hands him the field kit that opens High Point's inner gate — and the bill comes with it: remember everyone.

Panel 35

A radio on a café table, night. Everyone in frame is listening and no one is touching it. A calm, warm, reasonable voice comes out of the speaker — the first time we hear DANNY.

DANNY (radio): "The seal is mercy. The outside will burn this peninsula the moment it opens. I only ask High Point for the keys — so no one has to die proving it."

He offered power for Westlight's keys. Missy refused. Her grid was failing anyway. That's what made it a good offer.

Panel 36

A dead drop in the rain — a rusted tin under a piling. Ian's scarred hand takes out a folded note: patrol rotations, charge placements. Behind him, out of focus on a rooftop, a woman watches. Long dark hair. SARA.

Sara Lindgren. His first love. Now standing at Danny's side — feeding Ian the truth, one drop at a time.

Panel 37

Split panel. Left: Sara in Danny's camp, close at his shoulder like she belongs to him, a ledger under his arm with her name in it. Right: the same woman alone at night, folding another note with shaking hands.

The camp thought she was his. The truth: Danny held her life in his ledger, and she'd decided to spend it on warnings.

Panel 38

DANNY's camp from above — a tall masked figure among fires, face never shown, reading a patrol report. Beside him, Sara, not looking at the page she already knows by heart.

The deeper cut: Danny had known for weeks. He let the real intel flow to earn her trust. Then he started feeding her lies to pass along.

Panel 39

A bridge diagram on a war table, Ian's people around it, the plan drawn in confident lines. One annotation, in Sara's handwriting: EAST SPAN CHARGES — DEAD.

The east span charges were live. Danny held the detonator. And his men would not pull back at dawn. The lie rode all the way to the bridge — unless someone burned themselves to stop it.

CHAPTER FOUR — ACT III: REACHING MISSY CHANGES THE OBJECTIVE

Panel 40

HIGH POINT under brownout. Before Ian ever arrives, we see it through her hands: MISSY reroutes a breaker in the dark, settles a ration dispute with two sentences, climbs a black stairwell and pulls a child back from a breached door — alone, capable, exhausted.

Everyone spoke of Ian as if rescue were a person instead of a system. Missy was busy being the system.

Panel 41

The last courtyard, mid-attack. Ian comes through the siege line and stops: Missy is already there, fighting beside her people, a wrench in one hand and a flare in the other, entirely unsurprised that the world is ending.

He crossed nine districts of dark to save her. She was saving people when he got there.

Panel 42

After. Quiet. They stand inches apart in the ruined courtyard — too much history, no privacy, his filthy tank and her field gear, his burns and her shaking hands. The whole campaign fits in the space between two faces.

IAN: "I made it."

MISSY: "So did they."

Panel 43

One embrace — brief, hard, earned. Then Missy pulls back and presses a fuse into his hand like it's a ring.

MISSY: "You can hold me after we keep the east block alive."

IAN: "…What did they do to you — no. Tell me where it goes."

Panel 44

A community room lamplight. Missy, Samir, Ian around a table of repeaters and cable. Missy sets down a ring of heavy keys.

MISSY: "Westlight isn't a weapon. It's a radio protocol. Repeaters, trust, a signal nobody can fake."

Whoever holds the keys controls movement, food — and the story of why the bridge fell. That's why Danny wants them. That's why she won't give them up.

Panel 45

Sara comes in person — rain-soaked, having walked through Danny's lines to High Point, knowing what it costs. Ian is already moving toward the door, planning an extraction route out loud.

SARA: "A rescue tips him. He smells it, he moves the charges."

IAN: "I'm not leaving you there."

SARA: "Some people you save by leaving."

Panel 46

Night. A small room, two women, no Ian. Missy slides a key across the table — the west service corridor, a way out Ian doesn't know exists because Missy built it after he left.

MISSY: "If it goes wrong, you run that corridor. Don't wait for him."

SARA: "You love him."

MISSY: "Yes. Go save yourself."

Panel 47

The High Point roof. Ian and Missy look down at boats rocking black and useless on the water. The whole sealed city spreads below them in pockets of gold and dark.

IAN: "Boats. We could go by water."

MISSY: "Boats carry infection. And thousands stay."

He could stay only for her. Or stay because her work had become his. The difference would decide how the city fought — and how it ended.

Panel 48

WESTWOOD, the night before the bridge operation. The convoy staging ground. KEITH — seventy-two, white-haired, gentle — walks Ian down a line of porch lights he relights every night, even at the empty houses. His pencil ledger is in his coat.

KEITH: "Every name matters, Ian. Even the ones nobody's left to say."

IAN: "Then we carry them. All of them. Even me."

Panel 49

Headlights through rain. Danny's raiders hit the gate. The convoy has ninety seconds to live and Keith — unarmed — steps into the road and starts talking to the men coming to kill everyone, using their names.

KEITH: "Marcus. Your mother taught you to read at the kitchen table. Daniel — you sang in the—"

Panel 50

The convoy gets through. Keith goes down mid-sentence in the wet road, the ledger still in his hand. Ian reaches him too late and not too late: the old man's hand presses the book into Ian's chest with the last of his strength.

KEITH: "Don't let them be pencil."

Panel 51

Dawn. The staging ground empty, the gate open, porch lights still burning behind them. Ian stands with the ledger open in both hands, adding nothing, erasing nothing. Behind him, the districts' fighters are arriving — no longer helpers. An army.

After that night the districts stopped being helpers. They became an army. And the operation had a witness.

CHAPTER FIVE — ACT IV: EVERY ROAD REACHES THE BRIDGE

Panel 52

DELRIDGE at dawn — rail cuts, garages, drainage channels. JUNE ALVAREZ backs her armored utility truck out of a flooded bay, Ian riding the running board, two fingers of his right hand splinted straight from a crush injury. She has rebuilt his baton grip around them without comment.

JUNE: "Steel, fuel, one hour nobody shoots at me."

Delridge made the road. Westwood supplied the people. Every district arrived carrying something it had paid for.

Panel 53

Inside the span's service passage: MATEO RUIZ with a scanner against a charge housing, face gone gray. The charge is clean, military, and old — older than the outbreak.

MATEO: "It did not fall. It was made to fail."

The charges were placed before the outbreak reached the peninsula. A sealed field test. Witnesses included. Danny was left inside with orders — and turned them into a crown.

Panel 54

CHRIS on the span with his Counterweight rig, hands shaking over the controls, jokes gone quiet. Ian beside him, looking at two spans and one decision built on Sara's intel.

CHRIS: "Rig can drop either one. It can't tell me which one's lying."

Choose wrong, and the bridge operation pays in blood. The lie — or the truth — was about to surface at the worst possible altitude.

Panel 55

ALL LIGHTS. Night, the whole peninsula in one wide panel: café, clinic, garage, shelters, porch lights — every safehouse answering a roll call in warm gold windows, one by one, across the dark.

RAE (radio): "Alki. …Admiral. …Junction. …Morgan. …Lincoln. …Delridge. …Westwood. …High Point. All lights report."

On the broadcast table, open, sat Keith's ledger.

Panel 56

THE BROKEN SPAN. Narrow girders over black water, rain coming sideways, the city lit behind Ian and nothing ahead but dark. At the far end of the girder stands DANNY — tall, still, in dark tactical gear, his face a featureless mask we will never see under. Beside the approach, VOSS, his enforcer, all mass and patience, steps back at a small gesture. This is not his fight.

DANNY: "You open that channel and you sign their deaths. The math isn't cruel, Ian. It's just math."

IAN: "Your math. Not mine."

Panel 57

Phase one — THE ARGUMENT. They circle on the girder, testing footing, Danny controlled, almost gentle, a man still trying to win a debate at the edge of a drop.

DANNY: "Everyone you love is inside my arithmetic."

IAN: [a low sound, barely human] "Then I'll break it."

Panel 58

Phase two — THE SPAN FAILS. A girder section groans, sheds dust, and goes. Danny stops talking: a snapped cable swings like a scythe across the deck, debris kicked spinning toward the edge. He would rather drop Ian than lose the argument.

Panel 59

Phase three — THE EDGE. One final grapple, both men half over black water, rain in their faces, Ian's ruined hand locked on a cable, Danny's mask inches from Ian's face — blank, unreadable, never anything else.

Whoever was losing got one last hold. Ian's held.

Panel 60

THE CHOICE, drawn twice in mirror panels. Left: Ian hauls Danny up onto the deck — alive, mask on, hands bound; a confession that could air as proof, and loyalists who would bleed people trying to take him back. Right: Ian's fingers open over the water.

MISSY (radio, later, in the quiet version): "What did you leave down there?"

The game doesn't tell you which man Ian is. You do.

Panel 61

After. A girder strut below the span. Caught on the steel, empty, undamaged, facing the water: the mask. Ian looks at it for a long moment. He leaves it there.

The game never shows what was underneath. Some things the seal keeps.

Panel 62

THE LONG WALK. Ian and Missy carry the bridge transmitter together up the failing span, his bulk braced against the fractured mast, her hands on the cable runs. Danny's voice rides the radio the whole climb — from custody, or from old intercepts. It doesn't matter. It's the same words.

DANNY (radio): "You open that channel and you sign their deaths. You know I'm right."

Panel 63

The mast, the microphone, two people and an open ledger. Missy lays out the choice the way she lays out rations: quiet, no timer, no music. Everything they know on one side. Everyone they love on the other.

MISSY: "All of it, or the version that keeps them breathing. Choose like it's yours. It is."

Panel 64

FULL TRUTH. Ian at the microphone, looking like nine districts — burns, bandage, broken fingers, the tank that never came clean. Missy beside him, chin up: say it looking like that; let them see.

IAN (broadcast): "This is Ian. West Seattle. The bridge didn't fall. It was dropped — before the outbreak, on purpose, to seal us in. I have the proof. We're alive in here. If you burn us to bury that, know we knew you would — and we said it anyway."

Panel 65

CONTROLLED MESSAGE. The same mast, the same man, a different weight on him. The ledger closed under his hand like a door he's choosing to shut.

IAN (broadcast): "This is Ian. West Seattle. We're alive, we're organized, and we're asking for a corridor — food, medicine, a way out for the sick. We held the light on. Answer us."

Panel 66

On the strut below, overlooked by everyone but the reader: a girl's hair tie from a golden-hour summer, left on the steel where Ian fought Danny. No note. Sara never came back to the camp, and the camp is taken, and she is simply gone.

The game never confirms whether she made it out. Some people you save by leaving. Some people, that's the last thing they save you with.

Panel 67

THE ENDING, WIDE. Across West Seattle, warm lights answer the broadcast — windows, porches, the café, the clinic, High Point gold against the dark. Downtown stays distant. A single white light may or may not answer from across the water.

MISSY: "You crossed all that to find me."

IAN: "No. I crossed it so we could choose what happens next."

Panel 68

Final panel of the main story. A safehouse porch at night, two figures on watch — Ian and Missy, shoulders almost touching, the ledger closed on the rail between them, one practical light burning above the door. Rain. Quiet. The city is not saved.

It is no longer silent. The light stays on.

CHAPTER SIX — THE TURNED PATH

The second game. It begins with a bite — only ever a bite. Never a scratch, a fall, a bullet. Beaten unbitten, the story above is complete and canon. This is the other one.

Panel 69

A clinic corridor, close: teeth — a Walker's — closing on Ian's forearm as he holds a door for people escaping behind him. No drama. No slow motion. Just the cost of a held door.

The timer starts. There is no countdown anyone can see. Exertion feeds it. Rest starves it a little. Nothing stops it. Not even rage.

Panel 70

A four-panel deterioration strip. Fever, dark veins crawling from the bite as Ian stares at his own shaking hands. Then the growl coming easier in a doorway while allies step back. Then a blackout panel — pure black. Then Ian waking in the rain somewhere he doesn't know, blood under his nails that he doesn't remember earning.

MISSY (stage two, touching his face): "Your hands. Look at me — your hands are shaking and you're lying about it. Don't you lie to me, Ian."

Panel 71

THE TURN, mid-mission, no cutscene. One panel of Ian mid-stride — the next panel the same stride, finished by something else. Stronger. Faster. The UV handlamp falls from fingers it has started to burn.

Control does not cut to black. It continues — as infected-Ian. The world is now written in heartbeats and currents of smell. Human tools are gone. The voice is gone. The objective is not.

Panel 72

The city inverted: doors that opened for Ian, barred. Survivors fleeing from the shape of him. Safehouse gold light ahead — and it hurts; he shades his eyes from the warmth he built. Past the bars of one window, a kid he once escorted along the Alki seawall waves at him, uncertain.

He does not wave back. He can't. He keeps walking. That is the most human thing left in him: he keeps walking.

Panel 73

LINCOLN PARK. Jeff — twitchy, terrified, shaking head to foot — standing his ground in the green dark in front of infected-Ian, hands up, talking the whole time, refusing to run.

JEFF: "I know it's you in there. You don't get to leave me too."

Jeff walks him through the green dark one last time. It is the only guided sequence in this whole second game — and the quietest.

Panel 74

THE MAST. It stands above the city, its light still on, still waiting. And at the gate: Missy. She sees what he is. She understands exactly what it costs. She opens the gate anyway. No speech. She just steps aside.

It is the bravest thing in the game.

Panel 75

ENDING A — "THE LAST HUMAN ACT." At the microphone, mid-turn, Ian spends the last of his voice. Only the raw truth fits through what's left of it: the charges, the field test, the orders. No choice remains — the turn makes it for him. Missy holds the mast as the broadcast goes out and his voice goes quiet under it.

The city is not saved. It is no longer silent. Neither was he, at the end.

Panel 76

ENDING B — "SILENCE." The transmitter on the empty mast, its small light on, still waiting. Below, in the tree line, a shape that was Ian walks away from it into the green dark, unhurried. The panel's border closes to black around him.

No score. No verdict. The game does not tell you that you failed. It doesn't have to.

Panel 77

Last page. The two endings of the whole book side by side, divided by a gutter of rain: a lit porch with two figures on watch — and a dark mast with nobody coming. Same city. Same light, burning in both.

The standard path asks a living man to choose between truth and mercy. The Turned Path reveals the choice was always a luxury of the living. Either way — the light stays on.

SOLACE — Chaotic Designs. The city is sealed. The bridge is gone. The light stays on.
